name: Apache Thrift
baseline: gRPC (C++ server, grpc 1.x of early 2016, protoc 3.0.0)
workload: Round-trip latency of a minimal request/response service ('agent' proto/IDL) against a Thrift C++ server versus a gRPC C++ server, driven by a Go test client with one non-concurrent client (go test -bench . -benchtime 10s -cpu 1).
claimed_speedup: Single client, ns/op per call: Thrift C++ (Buffered Transport) 38221 vs gRPC C++ 113525, about 3.0x lower latency (derived from page data); Thrift C++ (Framed Transport) 42343 vs 113525, about 2.7x (derived from page data). Author's summary: 'Thrift is way faster but gRPC is way easier'. The 128-client run lists only gRPC C++ (58358 ns/op) and Go servers, no Thrift C++ row.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the Thrift C++ server (a prebuilt binary thrift/gen-cpp/servercpp, Thrift 0.9.3). gRPC C++ server built with g++ -std=c++11, no -O flag in server/Makefile, linked against prebuilt libgrpc++_unsecure; protoc 3.0.0.
hardware: Darwin 15.2.0, 2.5 GHz Intel Core i7 (4x2 cores with HT), 1600 MHz DDR3 RAM (exact CPU model not given)
tradeoffs: Thrift needs more hand-written boilerplate and generates much more code than gRPC (author counts 999 SLOC of Go versus 117 with grpc-go); the generated client is not concurrent and connections are not multiplexed; the out-of-the-box C++ server is single threaded, and the non-blocking server needs libthriftnb. gRPC gives HTTP/2 multiplexing, tracing and latency profiling by default.
caveats: Third-party hobby repo (1 star, BSD-3-Clause) from about 2016: Thrift 0.9.3, protoc 3.0.0, Go 1.5.2, macOS. Only the server side is C++; every client is the same Go test harness, so this measures Thrift C++ server plus Go Thrift client against gRPC C++ server plus Go gRPC client. Thrift C++ is a prebuilt binary with no build flags or compiler recorded, and the gRPC C++ server was compiled without optimisation flags (affects only the trivial handler). The author notes the Buffered Transport comparison is not like for like with gRPC (gRPC uses framing and extra bookkeeping); with Framed Transport Thrift Go is only about 15% faster than grpc-go. No concurrent-client row for Thrift C++ exists (its server is single threaded). Numbers are ten years old; modern gRPC releases are much changed. Thrift claims 'efficient' in the awesome-cpp list entry, but the project itself publishes no benchmark; this is the only numeric Thrift-versus-gRPC comparison reachable here.

name: CppCMS
baseline: WordPress on PHP 5.2 (lighttpd 1.4.13 + FastCGI, MySQL 5.0, WP-Cache-2); also Java Servlets/JSP blog in the project's other case study
workload: Full blog application (database access, text formatting, comment sanitation, caching) served through FastCGI, measured in page fetches per second with no cache and with varying cache miss ratios, CppCMS blog versus WordPress.
claimed_speedup: No cache: CppCMS 310 fetches/s vs WordPress 7.6 fetches/s, about 41x (derived from page data). Cache 0% miss ratio: CppCMS 2300 vs WordPress 711 req/s (about 3.2x, derived); 50% miss ratio: 570 vs 13 req/s (about 44x, derived). The page states more than 10x difference at 3% miss ratio and that the CppCMS blog beats the JSP and PHP blogs by an order of magnitude; the Java blog used about 30x and the PHP blog about 3x the memory of the CppCMS blog.
tradeoffs: Applications are compiled C++ with a template-to-C++ view compiler, so no scripting-style edit-and-reload; smaller ecosystem than PHP/Java; needs the bundled Booster library and a FastCGI/SCGI/HTTP front end.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: cppcms.com and blog.cppcms.com are blocked by the egress proxy here, so the benchmark pages were never opened; the figures come from WebSearch result summaries of the benchmarks_php page (one summary printed 3,100 fetches/s for CppCMS, two others 310; 310 is used because it repeated and matches the stated 'more than 10 times'). First-party, roughly 2008-era numbers (PHP 5.2, lighttpd 1.4.13, Athlon XP 64) comparing two different blog applications, not a controlled framework microbenchmark; the PHP side is WordPress with a cache plugin patched by the author, not a lean PHP script. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model are not stated in the summaries and benchmark code was not located in the repo (no benchmarks directory). The 'LGPLv3' tag in the awesome-cpp list is outdated: the repo README says MIT since 1.2. Cap at C.

name: Drogon
workload:
Hello-world HTTP response ('

Hello, world!

' from an HttpSimpleController on /benchmark, 16 Drogon threads) versus an nginx module returning the same body, load generated with httpress at 100/1000/10000 connections with and without keep-alive; each setting run five times, max and min recorded.
claimed_speedup: Keep-alive, kQPS Drogon vs nginx (max/min of 5 runs): 100 conns 561/552 vs 330/329; 1000 conns 573/565 vs 333/327; 10000 conns 512/508 vs 316/314, about 1.6x-1.7x (derived from page data). No keep-alive: 100 conns 140/135 vs 31/49; 1000 conns 155/143 vs 52/50; 10000 conns 143/141 vs 43/40, about 2.9x-4.5x (derived from page data). Page says Drogon 'has a clear advantage over nginx' and exceeds 500,000 requests/s with keep-alive.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 on CentOS 7.4; optimisation flags not stated
hardware: Dell server, two Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60 GHz (16 cores, 32 threads), 64 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Fully asynchronous callback API (C++14/17/20 with coroutine support) with a built-in ORM; heavier framework than a bare server; handler runs on a small thread pool so blocking calls stall the event loop.
caveats: First-party wiki page; Drogon side source is in the repo (examples/benchmark: BenchmarkCtrl.cc, main.cc) but the nginx hello_world module and nginx configuration are not published, compiler flags are not stated, and the placement of the httpress client (same host or not) is not stated. Nginx is run through a hand-written module rather than serving a static file, which is not the usual nginx deployment. The no-keep-alive nginx figures are inconsistent (31/49 where max is below min). Environment is CentOS 7.4 and gcc 7.3.0, so numbers are several years old. The author writes 'If someone does a more accurate test, please correct me.' The README also links the TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks and a search snippet says Drogon was first in Round 19 composite score; techempower.com, Wikipedia and Gigazine were blocked, so that independent evidence was not opened and is not used for the tier (it could lift the entry to B in a session that can reach it). The repo has since moved to drogonframework/drogon; an-tao/drogon still resolves.
